43678.title: Snow White and Rose Red
43678.caption: Richard Doyle. Snow White and Rose Red, n.d. The Art Institute of Chicago.
43678.alt: A work made of watercolor over graphite on ivory wove paper, laid down on card.
43678.short:
A fair-haired girl in a long pink-red dress leans against a large black bear lying on the grass, holding a sprig of white flowers up in one hand. A second girl, dressed in white with flowers in her hair, lies on her back beside the bear. On the right, under the trees, a figure in a red hooded cloak sits next to a spinning wheel. Behind them rise blue mountains, dark fir trees and trees in autumn colours. The title names the fairy tale of Snow White and Rose Red.

Richard Doyle made this small picture in watercolour over pencil on ivory paper.

22646.title: Two Old Men beside a Sled Bearing the Coats of Arms of Amsterdam and Utrecht
22646.caption: Hendric Avercamp. Two Old Men beside a Sled Bearing the Coats of Arms of Amsterdam and Utrecht, 1620/33. The Art Institute of Chicago.
22646.alt: A work made of opaque and translucent watercolors, with pen and brown ink, over graphite, on cream laid paper.
22646.short:
Hendrick Avercamp frequently depicted recreational activities on ice. But it is unclear whether the figures here are at leisure or work. The seated postman in blue may be concluding his daily rounds between Utrecht and Amsterdam (as the coats of arms at the back of his sled imply). His clothing is more formal than that of the older, standing men, which suggests that they come from different social classes. Behind these principal figures, workers push goods across the frozen river to tall ships in the distance.

Avercamp employed many different kinds of media to create this work and placed each element with care. He first drew the composition with graphite and then precisely applied different tones of watercolor with fine brushes. The resulting drawing effectively conveys frozen water, frigid air, and the sun setting against a northern sky.

26601.title: Bikuni Bridge in Snow (Bikunibashi setchu), from the series "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei)"
26601.caption: Utagawa Hiroshige. Bikuni Bridge in Snow (Bikunibashi setchu), from the series "One Hundred Famous Views of Edo (Meisho Edo hyakkei)", 1858. The Art Institute of Chicago.
26601.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; oban.
26601.short:
Snow falls against a deep blue sky in this street scene. On the left, a tall signboard painted with large black characters stands on a wooden trestle. In the middle, a figure in a wide straw hat walks towards a wooden bridge, carrying a load of pink boxes. Beyond the bridge, a stone wall is topped with snow-covered pine trees, and a tower rises in the distance. On the right, baskets hang under the snowy roof of a shop, beside a cart wheel, and two dogs stand in the snow.

This colour woodblock print by Utagawa Hiroshige comes from his series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo and is dated 1858.

77673.title: Three Friends of Winter
77673.caption: Helen Hyde. Three Friends of Winter, 1913. The Art Institute of Chicago.
77673.alt: A work made of color woodcut on cream japanese paper.
77673.short:
A small girl with black hair tied up on top of her head walks across a green floor, carrying a bowl that holds a miniature pine tree and a branch of pink plum blossom. She wears a dark kimono patterned in green and white. Behind her, grey sliding screens are decorated with white bamboo. On the floor to the left, a teapot sits on a small brazier.

The panel below the picture explains the title: "Pine: long life, family love, needles radiating from a common centre. Plum: grace and sweetness. Bamboo: purity, integrity, straight, white within. All for friendship that no winter storms can harm." Helen Hyde made this colour woodcut on Japanese paper in 1913.

130552.title: Kozuke Province: Mount Haruna in Snow (Kozuke, Harunasan setchu), from the series "Famous Places in the Sixty-odd Provinces (Rokujuyoshu meisho zue)"
130552.caption: Utagawa Hiroshige. Kozuke Province: Mount Haruna in Snow (Kozuke, Harunasan setchu), from the series "Famous Places in the Sixty-odd Provinces (Rokujuyoshu meisho zue)", 1853. The Art Institute of Chicago.
130552.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; oban.
130552.short:
Towering rocks covered in snow fill this mountain view, with snow still falling from a grey sky. A red wooden bridge arches over a deep gorge, where a blue stream runs between the rocks. Two small figures approach the bridge from the left. Above it, a red building with a snow-covered roof stands on top of a rock, and to the right a long building with an open veranda looks out over the gorge. Tall conifers covered in snow crowd the slopes behind.

This colour woodblock print by Utagawa Hiroshige, dated 1853, comes from his series Famous Places in the Sixty-odd Provinces.

109780.title: Love of Winter
109780.caption: George Wesley Bellows. Love of Winter, 1914. The Art Institute of Chicago.
109780.alt: Painting of a crowd of well-dressed light-skinned people in an open, snowy field surrounded by large rolling hills. At center a woman in a bright-yellow coat and skirt holds the hand of a child in red, who pulls to turn her toward the others.
109780.short: In January 1914 George Bellows wrote to a friend, “There has been none of my favorite snow. I must always paint the snow at least once a year.” Soon after, on February 13, a major blizzard hit New York City, inspiring the artist to paint Love of Winter. He used bright reds, yellows, and greens to intensify the winter scene and broad, slashing brushstrokes to convey movement, wind, and speed. The energetic group of skaters and onlookers, composed of people of a range of ages and social classes, reflects the diverse populations who enjoyed the public parks and the leisure activities they offered in early 20th-century New York City.

25743.title: The Adoration of the Magi
25743.caption: Raffaello Botticini. The Adoration of the Magi, c. 1495. The Art Institute of Chicago.
25743.alt: A work made of tempera on panel.
25743.short:
This round painting sets the Adoration of the Magi in front of a ruined classical building, with plants growing from its cracked stonework. Mary sits on the steps holding the Christ Child, and Joseph stands on a step beside them, leaning on a staff. One king kneels before them in a pink robe, with gifts on the ground nearby, while others in rich robes stand close by. Their followers crowd the scene with horses and a camel. A peacock perches on the roof on the right, an ox lies near the building, sheep stand in the foreground, and a small monkey sits on a stone block. In the distance on the left, a ship lies at anchor below rocky hills.

The museum attributes this tempera painting on panel to Raffaello Botticini and dates it to about 1495.

21682.title: Still Life
21682.caption: Pieter Claesz. Still Life, c. 1625. The Art Institute of Chicago.
21682.alt: A work made of oil on panel.
21682.short: Around 1600, as the Dutch economy boomed, large-scale still lifes depicting luxury goods emerged as a genre that appealed to a sophisticated clientele. Pieter Claesz. was a leading painter of a type of still life often described as a “banquet piece,” which featured sumptuous foods and opulent serving vessels, typically strewn across an elaborately dressed tabletop. These costly goods—like the lemon, olives, sweetmeats, and lace-edged damask tablecloth in this painting—were sometimes depicted in a state of decay to suggest the transitory nature of coveted earthly things. The well-preserved items here instead celebrate wealth and its lavish display.

16205.title: The Nativity
16205.caption: Perugino. The Nativity, 1500–05. The Art Institute of Chicago.
16205.alt: A work made of tempera on panel, transferred to canvas.
16205.short: These four panels, together with another one depicting the Resurrection (Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York), once constituted a predella—a series of small pictures, often narrative scenes, forming the base of an altarpiece. These predella scenes depict moments when Jesus’s divine nature was revealed: at his birth, at his baptism, during his conversation at a well with a Samarian woman, at his res-urrection, and through his appearance to Mary Magdalene after his resurrection. The painting that once surmounted the predella as the focal point of the altarpiece has not been identified.

109220.title: Annunciation to the Shepherds
109220.caption: After Jacopo Bassano. Annunciation to the Shepherds, c. 1710. The Art Institute of Chicago.
109220.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
109220.short:
An angel appears out of dark clouds at the top of this painting, above a group of shepherds and their animals. In the foreground, a man in a broad hat sits playing a pipe. Behind him, a young man leans over a sheep, and a woman kneels with her back to us beside a large brown cow. On the right, another man rests his head on his arm next to an ox. Goats and more sheep crowd around them, and a thick tree trunk rises on the left.

This oil painting was made around 1710, after a composition by Jacopo Bassano.

60294.title: New York Street
60294.caption: Childe Hassam. New York Street, 1902. The Art Institute of Chicago.
60294.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
60294.short: After studying painting in Paris, Childe Hassam applied the techniques of French Impressionism to his views of American cities and landscapes. While he also painted coastal and pastoral scenes, Hassam often focused on urban areas such as his hometown of Boston, and New York City, where he lived after returning from Paris. Here the artist rendered New York with short brushstrokes that emphasize the movement and activity of everyday life on Fifth Avenue along Central Park. He incorporated vivid colors, such as the red and yellow of the woman's hat and skirt, into what would otherwise be a predominantly gray and white winter cityscape and captured the light in a natural manner, presenting a picturesque view of a modern metropolis.

16648.title: Woman in Front of a Still Life by Cezanne
16648.caption: Paul Gauguin. Woman in Front of a Still Life by Cezanne, 1890. The Art Institute of Chicago.
16648.alt: A work made of oil on linen canvas.
16648.short:
The seated woman here remains unidentified, but the still-life painting dominating the background is well known: Paul Cezanne’s Still Life with Fruit Dish (1879–80; Museum of Modern Art, New York). Gauguin’s version is nearly the same scale as the original. In certain aspects of the compo-sition, Gauguin emulated Cezanne’s style, like the way he flattened the picture plane so that the woman appears to tip forward out of her chair.

Before becoming an artist, Gauguin was an art collector. Cezanne’s Still Life—one of five or six works by the artist in Gauguin’s collection—was a touchstone in his artistic education. It is possible that Cezanne referred to this work when he accused Gauguin of stealing his style, which he called his “petite sensation.”

This is one of thirty-five works that comprise the Winterbotham Collection. Click here to learn more about the collection.

93450.title: Winter Scene
93450.artist: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes
93450.caption: Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes. Winter Scene, c. 1786. The Art Institute of Chicago.
93450.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
93450.short: Two groups of working-class travelers, one with a slaughtered pig in tow, converge on an icy road during a snowstorm. Francisco de Goya captured the scene’s wintry atmosphere with barren trees, large swaths of cool grays and whites, and diagonal brushstrokes that convey rapid snowfall. This small painting is one of a series of studies Goya created for monumental tapestries depicting the four seasons, commissioned for a dining hall at the Royal Palace of El Pardo in Spain. The image would have been scaled up to life-size and then manufactured by weavers in Spain’s Royal Tapestry Factory.

16549.title: Apples and Grapes
16549.caption: Claude Monet. Apples and Grapes, 1880. The Art Institute of Chicago.
16549.alt: Apples and grapes rest in a shallow wicker basket on a table covered with a light-colored cloth. Additional fruit is scattered on the table.
16549.short: Claude Monet probably painted this and other still lifes in 1879–80, knowing that they would be more readily marketable than his landscapes. In Apples and Grapes, however, he employed the complexity of color, light, and texture found in his most Impressionist landscapes. This is particularly evident in the extensive cloth surface—the play of light on the horizontal brushstrokes (indicating the folds in the tablecloth) recalls earlier canvases in which Monet used similar short horizontals of variegated colors to suggest water rippling in the sunlight.

111059.title: Flowers and Fruit in a Porcelain Bowl
111059.caption: Juan de Zurbarán. Flowers and Fruit in a Porcelain Bowl, c. 1645. The Art Institute of Chicago.
111059.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
111059.short: Long assumed to be the work of Francisco de Zurbarán, the leading painter in Seville, Spain, this canvas is now considered to be by his son, Juan de Zurbarán, who specialized in exquisitely painted still lifes during his short career. The precise, sensuous application of paint and dramatic lighting are typical of Juan, whose style can be identified through only a few signed paintings. The expensive imported Chinese porcelain bowl would have appealed to the wealthy clientele who purchased his refined yet exuberant compositions.

64957.title: Grapes, Lemons, Pears, and Apples
64957.caption: Vincent van Gogh. Grapes, Lemons, Pears, and Apples, 1887. The Art Institute of Chicago.
64957.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
64957.short: This is one of a group of related canvases featuring seasonal fruit that Vincent van Gogh painted in the fall of 1887. In these works, he simplified his palette, employed more vibrant colors, and used a thicker, broader paint application than he had earlier. Here he explored the use of complementary colors—yellow and purple, blue and orange, and red and green—in the service of chromatic intensity. The effect of these color contrasts is heightened by the pulsating pattern of brushstrokes that defines the tablecloth and creates a force field around the fruit. The painting was probably among the “violent still lifes”—to quote Van Gogh’s friend the painter Emile Bernard—that he included in the group exhibition of young avant-garde artists that he organized at a local restaurant in November–December 1887.

65940.title: Still Life No. 3
65940.caption: Marsden Hartley. Still Life No. 3, 1923. The Art Institute of Chicago.
65940.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
65940.short:
A tabletop is crowded with fruit and pottery against a dark red background. On the left, a white fluted bowl is heaped with pears and other fruit. Behind it stand two jugs, a tall pink one with a curved handle and a darker red one, and to the right is a cream-coloured bowl with a small spout. More pears and round green fruit lie loose on the red-brown tablecloth. The shapes are painted with thick, visible brushstrokes and outlined in dark paint.

Marsden Hartley painted this oil on canvas in 1923.

265263.title: Still Life with Grapes and Flowers
265263.caption: Mélanie de Comoléra. Still Life with Grapes and Flowers, c. 1827. The Art Institute of Chicago.
265263.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
265263.short:
In this exquisite still life, Mélanie de Comoléra skillfully depicted a variety of flowers, fruits, and other luxury objects. On a marble ledge sits a wide bowl, overflowing with grapes and plums. Behind it, a glass pitcher holds a mix of colorful flowers. In the foreground, key limes and jalapeño peppers, botanical species that are not indigenous to Europe, evoke themes of colonialism and global trade.

Mélanie de Comoléra studied and worked in France before moving to London, where she made this painting. The artist established a successful career there and became the official painter to the Duchess of Clarence (later Queen Adelaide) and Queen Victoria.

6005.title: The Banks of the Marne in Winter
6005.caption: Camille Pissarro. The Banks of the Marne in Winter, 1866. The Art Institute of Chicago.
6005.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
6005.short: This painting of a rural winter landscape is resolutely un-picturesque. Its dark color palette is uninterrupted by any majestic natural elements, such as towering trees or a glittering pond. Even early in his career, Camille Pissarro subverted traditional landscape painting by deliberately diverging from the pastoral scenes of his mentor, Camille Corot. In this large, rectangular canvas, Pisarro applied paint heavily, often using a palette knife, in emulation of Gustave Courbet, whose work is on view nearby. Just a few years after he made this work, Pissarro adopted a more immediate approach to landscape painting, working en plein air (outdoors) directly from nature rather than in a studio, a technique closely associated with the Impressionists.

14647.title: Young Woman Sewing
14647.caption: Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Young Woman Sewing, 1879. The Art Institute of Chicago.
14647.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
14647.short: The model for this elegant painting of a French bourgeois woman sewing may be Aline Charigot, whom Pierre-Auguste Renoir would go on to marry. The artist treated his domestic subject—a middle-class woman embroidering a textile—with vibrant color, light-filled atmosphere, and freely handled paint. Cobalt blue dominates the composition with striking contrasts of red and spare touches of yellow, relying on the optical effect produced by the close proximity of primary colors to enliven the composition and increase the sense of direct observation and spontaneity.

19333.title: Kitchen Still Life
19333.caption: Paolo Antonio Barbieri. Kitchen Still Life, c. 1640. The Art Institute of Chicago.
19333.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
19333.short:
Food is set out on a plain wooden table against a dark background. A woven basket heaped with chestnuts stands at the centre. To the right, two round, flat cakes or loaves are stacked on a crumpled sheet of white paper. In the foreground lie three pale mushrooms, two of them turned over to show their gills, a small bunch of black grapes, and a grey plate of shelled nuts. The painter has picked out the weave of the basket and the shine on the chestnuts and grapes.

The museum attributes this oil painting to the Italian artist Paolo Antonio Barbieri and dates it to about 1640.

182381.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
182381.short: This painting by Severin Roesen, who immigrated to the United States from Cologne in 1848, features a profusion of berries, grapes, peaches, figs, and other fruits piled upon a marble slab. His composition is a celebratory display of nature’s bounty— portrayed in such minute detail as to feel artificial. Roesen worked in Pennsylvania, supported by German immigrants who operated local breweries there. While still lifes in the 19thcentury typically adorned domestic dining rooms, Roesen’s painting may have hung in a public tavern or restaurant. For such patrons, the artist probably painted pictures in exchange for beer. Roesen and his male patrons would not have been counted among the followers of the growing temperance movement in America at midcentury.

158320.title: Christmas Belles
158320.caption: Winslow Homer. Christmas Belles, published January 2, 1869. The Art Institute of Chicago.
158320.alt: A work made of wood engraving on paper.
158320.short: A party of women out in a sleigh fills this wood engraving, which Winslow Homer drew for the magazine Harper's Weekly; it was published on January 2, 1869. A man with a moustache and spectacles holds the reins at the front. Beside him sits a woman in a fur-trimmed coat, and four more women crowd in behind, one in a feathered hat turning to look back over her shoulder. A thick fur blanket hangs over the back of the sleigh, and the seat backs are decorated with a monogram. Sleigh bells hang from the horse's harness. Behind them, two men drive a second sleigh, and further back a child looks out from another sleigh while someone waves a white cloth. Bare winter trees line the snowy ground.

28875.title: Christmas
28875.caption: Samuel Palmer. Christmas, c. 1850. The Art Institute of Chicago.
28875.alt: A work made of etching on paper.
28875.short:
A full moon shines over a thatched cottage half hidden by trees. Light streams from its open doorway onto the path. In the foreground, a man in a hat drives a small flock of sheep along the lane, while a smaller figure stands nearby with a dog and another figure leans on the garden gate. A tall fir tree rises on the right against the night sky. The whole scene is built up from fine, dense lines that leave only the moon, the doorway and a few highlights bright.

Samuel Palmer made this etching, titled Christmas, around 1850. It is signed "S. Palmer" in the lower right corner.

54305.title: Christmas Time
54305.caption: George Baxter. Christmas Time, 1859. The Art Institute of Chicago.
54305.alt: A work made of steel engraving printed in black, with block printing in colors, on wove paper, varnished, laid down.
54305.short:
A boy stands on a shaggy rug just inside an open front door, wrapped against the cold in a cap, a long knitted scarf pulled up over his mouth, a brown coat and heavy boots with snow on them. A large bundle of holly is tied to his back with a rope, and beside him on the floor is a basket of fruit. From the right, a hand reaches into the picture, holding out a plate with a slice of cake and a small glass of dark red drink. Through the doorway lies a snowy garden with iron railings and small birds in flight.

George Baxter made this print in 1859. It combines a steel engraving printed in black with colours printed from blocks, and the surface is varnished.

59656.title: Winter, also called The Small Winter
59656.caption: George Baxter. Winter, also called The Small Winter, 1849. The Art Institute of Chicago.
59656.alt: A work made of steel etching, aquatint, and stipple printed in purple, with block printing in colors, on wove paper.
59656.short:
Frost covers the trees and bushes around an old water mill with a thatched roof and a large wooden wheel. Water spills through a wooden sluice gate under a narrow footbridge into a frozen pond. In the foreground, a little girl in a blue dress stands on the ice next to a small child sitting in the snow, and a girl in red stands among the frosted reeds on the right. A man in a top hat looks down from the mill wall. Tall bare trees rise against a pale sky, and the word "Winter" is engraved below the picture.

George Baxter made this print in 1849. It combines etching, aquatint and stipple printed in purple with colours printed from blocks.

25428.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; oban.
25428.short:

Small figures with umbrellas walk across the snowy courtyard, past stone lanterns and a gateway. In the middle, a white-blossomed tree is covered in snow, and on the right the view opens out over the snowy rooftops of the city below.

This colour woodblock print by Utagawa Hiroshige, made around 1840 to 1842, comes from his series Famous Places in the Eastern Capital.

81640.title: Snowy Landscape with Strollers
81640.caption: Kitao Masayoshi (Kuwagata Keisai). Snowy Landscape with Strollers, 1790s. The Art Institute of Chicago.
81640.alt: A work made of color woodblock print.

Some carry bundles or bags, some lean on walking sticks, and one carries a load of branches on his back. On the right, pine trees and red-tinged shrubs grow on a rocky slope. Across the water, a village sits on the far shore, and pale mountains line the horizon.

Kitao Masayoshi (also known as Kuwagata Keisai) made this colour woodblock print in the 1790s.

22442.title: Five Young Boys Rolling a Large Snowball
22442.caption: Isoda Koryusai. Five Young Boys Rolling a Large Snowball, c. 1772. The Art Institute of Chicago.
22442.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; chuban.
22442.short:
Five boys work together to roll an enormous snowball across the snow. One boy on the right and another bending low in front pull on a rope wrapped round the ball. A third boy holds a long bamboo pole, a fourth looks up over the top of the ball, and a fifth, at the back, holds his hands to his mouth as if to warm them. Above them hang branches weighed down with snow, and a tree trunk leans in from the left. The boys wear patterned clothes in soft greens and oranges, and the boy on the right wears wooden sandals.

The museum attributes this colour woodblock print to Isoda Koryusai and dates it to about 1772.

20965.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; chuban.
20965.short:
Two young women and a girl gather round a large dog made of snow. The girl reaches up to the snow dog's face, and a young woman bends over it, resting a hand on its head. Behind them are snow-covered pine branches and bushes, a red post rises at the top right, and the sky is printed in warm yellow.

Suzuki Harunobu made this colour woodblock print around 1767 to 1768. It is signed on the right.

21937.title: Adoration of the Magi
21937.caption: Jan van Scorel. Adoration of the Magi, c. 1519. The Art Institute of Chicago.
21937.alt: A work made of oil on panel.
21937.short: One of Jan van Scorel’s earliest known works, this image of three kings from distant lands paying tribute to the newborn Jesus incorporates elements of northern and southern European visual traditions. The refined landscape, intricate costumes, and individualized faces of the figures attest to lessons the artist likely learned from his Netherlandish predecessors. The elaborate architectural carvings, on the other hand, recall ancient Roman wall decoration. Van Scorel likely made this work while traveling to study in Italy: the panel on which it is painted is made of fir, a wood rarely used in the Low Countries but one he might have encountered on his way across the Alps. Van Scorel was praised by the first biographer of Netherlandish artists as the “lantern bearer” who brought the Italian Renaissance style back to Northern Europe.

111441.title: The Adoration of the Magi
111441.caption: Workshop of Cornelis Engebrechtsz.. The Adoration of the Magi, 1515-25. The Art Institute of Chicago.
111441.alt: A work made of oil on panel.
111441.short: The half-length format of this jewel-like painting makes the subject of the adoration of the Christ Child accessible, while the departure of the magi and their exotic followers enlivens the rocky landscape of the background. This picture was probably made for the market of discriminating private collectors just developing in the Low Countries in the early 16th century. Cornelis Engebrechtsz. worked in the northern city of Leiden but apparently made this small painting for export and sale in the more cosmopolitan southern provinces of the Low Countries, then the center of the emerging art market. Its design was copied in several paintings and illuminations made in Bruges.

158368.caption: Winslow Homer. A Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year, published December 24, 1859. The Art Institute of Chicago.
158368.alt: A work made of wood engraving on paper.
158368.short:

In the centre, a round picture shows the Nativity, with Mary holding the Christ Child while an old man kneels before them and others look on. The lower half shows a Christmas party: children dance in a ring while adults watch, and a decorated Christmas tree stands on the right.

Winslow Homer made this wood engraving, which was published on December 24, 1859.

15496.title: The Nativity
15496.artist: Master of the Historia Friderici et Maximiliani
15496.caption: Master of the Historia Friderici et Maximiliani. The Nativity, 1507–10. The Art Institute of Chicago.
15496.alt: A work made of oil on panel.
15496.short: Once thought to be by the young Albrecht Altdorfer, this painting is instead the work of a painter named after a winged altarpiece in the town of Pulkau, near the Austrian and Moravian border. Though the artist takes his name from the Pulkau altarpiece, he was probably active in Vienna. Like other loosely associated South German and Austrian artists of the early 16th century, who are now grouped together as the Danube School, the Master of Pulkau used exuberant natural forms to give a heightened emotional quality to his work. In this altarpiece wing, the swirling vegetation, excited angels, and oversized Virgin and animals direct the viewer’s attention to the vulnerable Christ Child, who is the focus of adoration.

105660.title: Approach to Christmas
105660.caption: George Hunt. Approach to Christmas, n.d. The Art Institute of Chicago.
105660.alt: A work made of aquatint, with hand-coloring, on cream wove paper.
105660.short: Snow falls on a broad street lined with brick houses in this hand-coloured aquatint, engraved by George Hunt after a painting by James Pollard. Horse-drawn coaches crowd the road. The largest carries passengers in top hats on its roof, along with luggage and a bundle of evergreen branches with red berries, and dead birds and other game hang from its sides. The coach is lettered with the names Sudbury, Norwich and Bury. Snow lies on the roofs and frosts the trees, and shop signs advertise rum, brandy and wines. In the lower right corner, a group of boys rolls a giant snowball while another bends to make a snowball of his own. At the lower left, a woman stands with a boy and a small dog.

149018.title: Nativity in an Initial H
149018.caption: Zanino di Pietro. Nativity in an Initial H, 1430/40. The Art Institute of Chicago.
149018.alt: A work made of brush and gouache, heightened with gum arabic, gold leaf, and gold paint, over brush and black ink, on vellum.
149018.short:
This Nativity is painted on vellum inside a large initial letter H, framed by leafy blue, green and red ornament and gold leaf. Mary kneels on the left in a blue cloak dotted with gold, her hands together in prayer. The Christ Child lies on the ground before her, surrounded by golden rays, and Joseph stands on the right in a yellow cloak. Behind them, under a wooden shelter with a straw roof, an ox and a donkey look out over a manger filled with hay. A gold star sends a ray down towards the child, and two groups of angels with gold haloes pray at the upper right. Beyond the shelter rise green hills with fields, buildings and a castle on a peak.

It was made by Zanino di Pietro in the Veneto region of Italy, between 1430 and 1440.

71532.alt: A work made of manuscript cutting in tempera and gold leaf on parchment, with gothica textualis inscriptions in black ink, verso.
71532.short:

Joseph stands on the left with a walking stick, in a blue hat and red cloak, and Mary kneels beside him in a blue mantle with her hands together. On the right, under a shelter with a green roof, the Christ Child lies wrapped in the manger, which has woven green sides. An ox and a donkey lean over him, two angels look down from behind the roof, and sheep graze below. Trees and buildings appear in the background, and a small star shines at the top.

This cutting from a choir book is painted in tempera and gold leaf on parchment. The museum gives it to the Master of the Brussels Initials and dates it to about 1390.

54287.short:

Shepherds crowd in from the right: one holds a crook, an old man and a young man lean close, and a man with a red cloth over his shoulder kneels with a small child. 156596.title: Fruit Piece
156596.caption: Hannah Brown Skeele. Fruit Piece, 1860. The Art Institute of Chicago.
156596.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
156596.short:
This pristinely arranged still life by Hannah Brown Skeele features US-grown produce as well as imported specialties such as bananas, oranges, a pineapple, and sugar cubes. The composition was likely to appeal to middle- and upper-class consumers in the mid-19th century, who increasingly purchased still-life paintings to adorn their homes. Born in Maine and active in Missouri, Skeele exhibited Fruit Piece the year it was painted, then already in the collection of a Saint Louis businessman.

The tropical fruits and sweetener were products of empire. Enslaved and indentured laborers of color cultivated such crops in the West Indies and Central and South America. The goods were transported from those regions to New Orleans and then northward along the Mississippi River.

131407.title: Wine, Cheese, and Fruit
131407.caption: John F. Francis. Wine, Cheese, and Fruit, 1857. The Art Institute of Chicago.
131407.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
131407.short: Succulent grapes, crumbling cheese, sparkling wine in elegant glasses, and cognac in tumblers are depicted in this opulent dessert picture by John Francis. Originally an itinerant portrait painter, Francis turned to still life in the mid-19th century when the availability of daguerreotype portraits rendered his trade obsolete. The penchant for household embellishment among the Victorian middle class created a lively market for still-life paintings, which were often hung in dining rooms. While spirits are featured prominently in this painting, the glasses that are less than half full and the presence of the water indicate balance and restraint, referring to the mid-century growth of the temperance movement, which promoted the ideals of moderation and self-control.

193362.title: The Nativity, in Coffer
193362.caption: Master of the Unicorn Hunt. The Nativity, in Coffer, c. 1490. The Art Institute of Chicago.
193362.alt: A work made of woodcut in black, hand colored with brush, stencil and watercolor on ivory laid paper mounted on the inside cover of a coffer, constructed of wood, iron, leather, horsehair and linen.
193362.short: This woodcut and coffer demonstrate the very unusual survival of a print in its original context. Incredibly, ten other impressions of this stencil-colored, mass-produced Nativity survive, all also in boxes, and approximately one hundred other French coffers ornamented with similar prints exist. Their original purpose, however, remains uncertain. Despite their metal reinforcements and standardized lock, they were not sturdy enough to be strapped to pack animals. They may instead have been worn as backpacks, with the cushion on the bottom allowing the container to sit on the traveler’s knees for use as a movable shrine. A shallow secret compartment in the lid of this example is equally mysterious. 44065.title: Just Dessert
44065.caption: William Michael Harnett. Just Dessert, 1891. The Art Institute of Chicago.
44065.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
44065.short: One of only three works William Michael Harnett painted in the year before his death, Just Dessert offers the viewer a display of foodstuffs sumptuously arranged on a marble surface. The traditional tabletop composition is one that Harnett often employed in his still lifes. In Just Dessert, the exotic clashes with the quotidian—Maraschino liqueur, half a coconut, and Smyrna figs rest alongside a copperpitcher, pewter tankard, and ginger jar. Small crumbs of cork are visible on the grapes and fig seeds are smashed on the side of the wooden box, indicating that the dessert has been eaten, as well as highlighting Harnett’s skillful renderings in trompe l’oeil (fool-the-eye) painting.

94126.title: Still Life with Monkey, Fruits, and Flowers
94126.caption: Jean-Baptiste Oudry. Still Life with Monkey, Fruits, and Flowers, 1724. The Art Institute of Chicago.
94126.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
94126.short: Jean-Baptiste Oudry received numerous commissions from Louis XV of France, who admired his skill as a painter of animals and still lifes. The artist frequently combined his two specialties, as in this work, in which a monkey, an animal celebrated in this period for its mischievous and lustful character, snatches a few grapes. The French Rococo taste for the sensual is manifest in the lush, overripe quality of the fruits and flowers, reminiscent of 17th-century Flemish works that Oudry is known to have studied. Paintings such as this typically adorned dining rooms as part of an overall decorative scheme.

A woman looks out from a balcony on the right, sparrows perch on the roof, and a plum tree blossoms above the fence.

This colour woodblock print by Kitagawa Utamaro is a double-page illustration from the poetry anthology The Young God Ebisu, published for the New Year of 1789.

The colour woodblock print, from the series Fashionable Genji, was designed by Utagawa Kunisada I and Utagawa Hiroshige around 1853.

Mary sits on a stone step holding the Christ Child, who reaches towards an old king with a white beard kneeling before them in a golden robe. The kneeling king offers a golden vessel. Behind him, a second king in a red robe holds up a gold cup, and a third, in a green cloak with a sword at his side, steps forward from the right. Joseph stands on the left. Ruined arches rise behind the group, and pale mountains appear in the distance. A handwritten inscription runs along the lower edge.

This watercolour over pencil was made in 1827 after a painting by Bonifazio de' Pitati, called Bonifazio Veronese.

This oil painting by an unknown French artist dates from between 1780 and 1790.

75507.title: Still Life: Corner of a Table
75507.caption: Henri Fantin-Latour. Still Life: Corner of a Table, 1873. The Art Institute of Chicago.
75507.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
75507.short: This canvas, exhibited at the Salon of 1873, relates to Henri Fantin-Latour’s largest and most famous painting of the decade, The Corner of a Table (1872; Musée d’Orsay, Paris), an immense composition that includes detailed portraits of several young Parisian poets and writers. The table around which they are posed displays many of the still-life elements featured in this work. The delicate rhododendron plant reflects the influence of Japanese prints, from its dramatic silhouette against the neutral backdrop of the white tablecloth to its unusual placement in the foreground, emphasizing the scene’s unorthodox cropping.

120154.title: Still Life—Strawberries, Nuts, &c.
120154.caption: Raphaelle Peale. Still Life—Strawberries, Nuts, &c., 1822. The Art Institute of Chicago.
120154.alt: Still life painting of strawberries, nuts, lemon, and porcelain vessels.
120154.short: A member of a prominent artistic family from Maryland and Pennsylvania, Raphaelle Peale was one of the first painters in the United States to specialize in still life. In this precisely arranged composition, he meticulously rendered the various surfaces and forms of fruits, nuts, and tableware. Influenced by 17th-century Dutch still lifes, Peale featured imported material goods, such as Chinese porcelain made for the American market, a luxury item symbolizing the increasing power and prosperity of the new nation. The large glass urn may hold strawberries grown out of season in greenhouses, called hothouses, an experiment undertaken at the family’s farm outside of Philadelphia.

184371.title: The Nativity
184371.caption: Fra Bartolommeo. The Nativity, 1504–7. The Art Institute of Chicago.
184371.alt: A light-skinned man in red and woman in blue sit with an infant between them, angels beside and above them, a small town in the background.
184371.short: To develop his own intimate style, Fra Bartolommeo looked to the most lyrical and harmonious paintings of his fellow artists working in Florence in the first years of the 16th century, including Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Raphael. When the young artist came under the spell of the ardent Dominican reformer Girolamo Savonarola in 1500, he abandoned his artistic career for several years to join the order, becoming Fra (Friar) Bartolommeo. He made this work after his return to painting in 1504, investing it with a new spirituality.

86998.title: Sandvika, Norway
86998.caption: Claude Monet. Sandvika, Norway, 1895. The Art Institute of Chicago.
86998.alt: Light-colored snowscape with visible brushstrokes featuring a bridge in front of red and white barns and farmhouses, surrounded by trees.
86998.short: Claude Monet’s trip to Norway in 1895 was perhaps the most physically taxing of all his many painting campaigns. Touring the country with his stepson Jacques Hoschedé, who lived in Christiania (now Oslo), he was awestruck but initially frustrated in his search for good motifs amid the snow. Nevertheless, he painted 29 Norwegian scenes during a two-month stay. These included at least six views of Sandvika, a village near Christiania whose iron bridge may have reminded Monet of the Japanese bridge at his home in Giverny.

51577.title: The White Tablecloth
51577.caption: Jean Siméon Chardin. The White Tablecloth, c. 1731–32. The Art Institute of Chicago.
51577.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
51577.short: Jean Siméon Chardin won acclaim for the still lifes and quiet scenes of middle-class domestic life that he exhibited at salons sponsored by the French Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture. In early still lifes like this one, he incorporated motifs common to 17th-century Dutch and Flemish works: the foreshortened knife, the handle of which protrudes over the table’s edge; the overturned glass; and the remains of a meal. The work’s unusual shape reveals its original function as a screen for the opening of a fireplace. Viewed at floor level, the screen would have conveyed the illusion of a table recessed into the fireplace.

The Art Institute of Chicago.
29544.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; oban.
29544.short:
Mount Fuji rises white against a blue sky in the upper left, with a second mountain below it, and a band of yellow light glows along the horizon on the right. In the foreground, two travellers cross the snow towards an arched wooden bridge. One wears a straw raincoat and a wide hat and carries a load on a pole; the other, in a brown coat, walks ahead. Tall pines heavy with snow stand beside a winding river, a second bridge crosses it further back, and thatched houses sit under thick snow on either side.

This colour woodblock print by Utagawa Hiroshige, dated 1855, is number 13 in his series Famous Sights of the Fifty-three Stations, also known as the Vertical Tokaido.

60651.title: Parody of Liu Bei (J: Gentoku) Visiting Zhuge Liang (J: Komei) in Wind and Snow (Gentoku fusetsu ni Komei o tazureru)

60651.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; oban triptych.
60651.short:
Three women make their way through falling snow across three joined sheets. On the left, a woman stands in front of a red building and snowy shrubs, holding a closed umbrella with a black-and-white pattern. In the middle, a woman bends into the wind under an open umbrella, her patterned kimono blowing around her. On the right, a woman with a scarf over her head carries a tray with a large bowl. Snowy hills and trees stretch across the background.

Utagawa Kunisada I made this colour woodblock triptych around 1844. Its title presents the scene as a parody of Liu Bei visiting Zhuge Liang in wind and snow.

2156.title: Lights of Other Days
2156.caption: John Frederick Peto. Lights of Other Days, 1906. The Art Institute of Chicago.
2156.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
2156.short: Lights of Other Days, like many of John F. Peto’s still lifes, is replete with nostalgia. Strewn along a shallow shelf above a doorframe is an array of old, well-worn objects: candleholders with wax candles nearly used up, rusty oil lamps, and torn books. These discarded commonplace objects allude to older ways of life and fading memories. Peto specialized in trompe l’oeil (fools the eye) pictures; yet his soft-edged style is suggestive of the artist’s hand rather than the heightened illusionism employed by other trompe l’oeil painters such as William Harnett. Trained in Philadelphia, Peto stopped exhibiting his work at professional venues by 1890, creating compositions instead for local patrons near his New Jersey home.

A tall tower stands among snowy pines on the hill at the top right, and a pagoda rises in the distance on the left.

This colour woodblock print by Utagawa Hiroshige, made around 1843 to 1847, comes from his series Famous Places in the Eastern Capital.

Snow-laden pines and other trees stand on both sides, with snowy roofs behind the fence.

This colour woodblock print by Utagawa Hiroshige, made around 1834, comes from his series Famous Places in Kyoto.

21687.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; three left sheets of oban pentaptych.
21687.short:

On the right, a woman carries a tray of cups, another kneels by a wooden bucket, and a folding screen painted with bamboo leans against stacked floor mats. Large paper lanterns with a leaf crest hang from the ceiling.

This colour woodblock print by Kitagawa Utamaro, made in the late 1790s, is made up of the three left sheets of a set of five.

59615.alt: A work made of steel etching, aquatint, and stipple printed in blue, with block printing in colors, on wove paper, laid down on card.

This print by George Baxter, from Ascent of Mont Blanc, is dated 1855. It combines etching, aquatint and stipple printed in blue with colours printed from blocks.

24418.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; center right sheet of oban pentaptych (three left sheets: 1928.1080).

Four women in patterned kimonos stand on a terrace of a temple. Three stand close together on the left, and a fourth, on the right, points at a large black lacquered structure covered with a pink cloth. Behind them rises a tall pine tree, and long covered walkways lead off into the temple grounds, where small figures walk across an open courtyard. A large black barrel bound with rope stands on the right.

Utagawa Toyohiro made this colour woodblock print around 1804 to 1810. It is the centre right sheet of a set of five, and it is signed "Toyohiro ga".

21174.caption: Isoda Koryusai. Puppies in the Snow, c. 1773. The Art Institute of Chicago.
21174.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; chuban.
21174.short:
A heap of puppies huddles together in the snow. Some are white, some spotted with black, and one is orange; a few sleep curled up while others look out. Behind them grow white daffodils with long green leaves. Above, snow lies along the edge of a thatched roof, snowflakes fall against a green sky, and soft yellow clouds frame the top of the picture.

Isoda Koryusai made this colour woodblock print around 1773. It is signed on the left.

7578.caption: Kitao Shigemasa. The Big Snowman, c. 1764. The Art Institute of Chicago.
7578.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; mizu-e hosoban.
7578.short:

A child on the left covers their face with both hands, another leans in from the right, and two more run up from the front. The children wear loose clothes in pinks and greens, and lines of flowing calligraphy run down from the top of the sheet. The soft colours are printed without black outlines.

Kitao Shigemasa made this colour woodblock print in a narrow upright format around 1764. It is signed at the lower right.

87073.caption: Utagawa Hiroshige. Sparrows and Camellia in Snow, c. 1837/48. The Art Institute of Chicago.
87073.alt: A work made of color woodblock print; tanzaku.
87073.short:
Two sparrows fly and perch among the branches of a camellia in falling snow. One swoops down from above with its wings spread, and the other sits on a branch below, looking up with its beak open. Snow lies thickly on the dark green leaves and on the bright red camellia flowers. The sky darkens to black at the top of this tall, narrow print.

Utagawa Hiroshige made this colour woodblock print around 1837 to 1848. It is signed "Hiroshige fude".

45838.title: Snow at Louveciennes
45838.caption: Camille Pissarro. Snow at Louveciennes, c. 1870. The Art Institute of Chicago.
45838.alt: A work made of oil on panel.
45838.short: Camille Pissarro made this small oil on panel painting showing trees and houses blanketed by a heavy snow at Louveciennes, the village west of Paris where he lived. Using a limited palette of shades of white, brown, blue, tan, gray, and green to evoke the gray skies and freshly fallen snow of a cold winter day, Pissarro created a scene that has the freshness and spontaneity of a work painted outdoors. Only the footsteps of a solitary figure, walking below the screen of trees, break the silence of this intimate and poetic winter scene.

497.title: A Mother Feeding her Child (The Happy Mother)
497.caption: Willem van Mieris. A Mother Feeding her Child (The Happy Mother), 1707. The Art Institute of Chicago.
497.alt: Painting of a scene in a dimly-lit, cavernous room with a bassinet and small table. A shaft of light falls on four figures: a light-skinned woman in a white head covering, a baby on her lap, a male figure at her side, and a small dog at their feet. The couple feeds the fussing baby from a bowl, smiling.
497.short: In this scene of domestic life, Willem van Mieris employed the highly finished, enamel-like technique known as fine painting to achieve a surface that shows no obvious traces of brushwork. While painters like Gerard ter Borch and Caspar Netscher reserved this time-consuming style for rare and expensive textiles like silk, Van Mieris applied it to more commonplace materials. Here, for instance, the artist deftly applied highlights to the cane bassinet and ceramic pitcher on the table with the tip of his brush.

151899.title: Illuminated Border with Bird, Strawberries and Flowers from a Choir Book
151899.caption: Unknown illuminator. Illuminated Border with Bird, Strawberries and Flowers from a Choir Book, n.d. The Art Institute of Chicago.
151899.alt: A work made of manuscript cutting in tempera, colored inks and gold leaf on vellum.
151899.short:
This tall, narrow strip of decoration once formed part of the border of a choir book page. At the top, curling blue and red leaves twist round each other. Below them grows a stem of flowers: a red carnation, a white daisy, a purple four-petalled flower, a blue star-shaped flower and others, with two ripe red strawberries. A small bird with a pinkish crest and a long beak perches in the middle. The background is scattered with tiny gold and black dots, and a gold band frames the edge.

This manuscript cutting is painted in tempera, coloured inks and gold leaf on vellum. The museum records it as European and does not give a date.

16629.title: Fruits of the Midi
16629.caption: Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Fruits of the Midi, 1881. The Art Institute of Chicago.
16629.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
16629.short:
A blue-and-white dish is heaped with fruit and vegetables: lemons, pomegranates, purple aubergines and green leaves. More lie on the white cloth in front of it, including a large aubergine, red and orange peppers, tomatoes and a pomegranate. The background is painted in soft, blurred greens and blues, and short, lively brushstrokes catch the light on each surface.

Pierre-Auguste Renoir painted this oil on canvas in 1881. It is inscribed "Renoir 81" in the lower left corner.

62450.title: Still Life with a Basket of Fruit and a Bunch of Asparagus
62450.caption: Louise Moillon. Still Life with a Basket of Fruit and a Bunch of Asparagus, 1630. The Art Institute of Chicago.
62450.alt: Painting of a woven basket filled with various fruits, including plums and apricots, on a table against a dark background, with asparagus and peapods on the table at front.
62450.short:
At a time when still life was emerging as a discrete subject (and not just an element of larger narrative works), this artist depicted fruit and vegetables arrayed on a simple tabletop with elegant clarity and naturalism. Louise Moillon trained first under her father and, from 1620, her stepfather. When she executed this still life at the young age of 20, she was already an accomplished painter.

Women painters were not uncommon within the European tradition of the family workshop, which provided training, studio space, and clients for successive generations of artists. The system was one of few pro- fessional routes for women in a period when they could not legally take up a career.

27952.alt: A work made of oil on panel.
27952.short:
A thick slice of orange melon stands upright on the left. On the right is a green glazed jar with a handle over the top and a small spout. In front of them, two fish lie side by side on a sheet of yellow paper on the table. The paint is laid on thickly in short, dense strokes, with dark outlines round each object. The name "Vincent" is painted in the lower left corner.

This oil painting on panel is dated around 1888. The museum describes its painter as an imitator of Vincent van Gogh.

257286.title: Breakfast Still Life
257286.caption: Willem Claesz. Heda. Breakfast Still Life, 1647. The Art Institute of Chicago.
257286.alt: A work made of oil on panel.
257286.short: This still life may look like a snapshot of an abandoned meal, but the scene is carefully arranged, revealing the artist’s ability to create complex but harmonious compositions with a limited palette of neutral colors. William Claesz. Heda balanced the horizontal pewter chargers in the foreground with the vertical glass vessels and salt-cellar in the background and positioned the overturned ewer diagonally to connect the two planes. Faint creases in the tablecloth, plates hanging precariously off the table’s edge, and the window reflected on the pitcher’s surface demonstrate the artist’s observant eye as well as his virtuosity in handling paint.

21934.title: Kitchen Scene
21934.caption: Diego Velázquez. Kitchen Scene, 1618–20. The Art Institute of Chicago.
21934.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
21934.short: In this modest kitchen scene, a type known as a bodegón (from the Spanish word for pantry), Diego Velázquez depicted a young African woman at work, surrounded by exquisitely rendered pots, jugs, a mortar and pestle, and a crumpled paper wrapper for spices. In creating this painting, Velázquez may have used an enslaved woman from his or an associate’s household as a model. Slavery was widespread in the young artist’s hometown of Seville, Spain, and Velázquez, his father, and his teacher, Francisco Pacheco, were all enslavers.

154496.title: Rack Picture for Dr. Nones
154496.caption: William A. Mitchell. Rack Picture for Dr. Nones, 1879. The Art Institute of Chicago.
154496.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
154496.short: This type of trompe l’oeil (fools the eye) painting simulates an old-fashioned bulletin board that held important, yet ephemeral documents like letters and newspaper clippings under strips of ribbon. Such “rack picture” still lifes functioned as biographical portraits, in this case for Dr. Samuel Smith Nones, the prominent Philadelphia dentist who commissioned this work. Adjacent to the central letter to Dr. S. S. Nones are envelopes addressed to medical colleagues and one to Nones’s brother. The painting’s illusionistic fragments cleverly define the dentist’s professional and personal identity, narrating a rich tale of camaraderie and achievement for an inner circle of viewers. William A. Mitchell, the father of the youngest dentist in the group, likely executed the composition.

39954.title: Seventeenth-Century Interior
39954.caption: Charles Gifford Dyer. Seventeenth-Century Interior, 1877. The Art Institute of Chicago.
39954.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
39954.short: Chicagoan Charles Gifford Dyer studied painting in Paris and Munich. The objects depicted here, such as the Chinese blue-and-white vase and Oushak Turkish rug, were likely collected during his extensive travels and represent the tastes of a worldly, wealthy man. The composition recalls 17th-century Dutch still lifes in its focus on surfaces, textures, and illusionism. Similarly, it evokes the fleetingness of life by juxtaposing items that quickly decay, such as fruit and flowers, with the enduring arts of literature and music.

27992.title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884
27992.caption: Georges Seurat. A Sunday on La Grande Jatte — 1884, 1884–86, border added 1888–89. The Art Institute of Chicago.
27992.alt: Large painting of people in a crowded park, brushstrokes are dots.
27992.short:
In Ferris Bueller’s Day Off, Ferris’s best friend Cameron Frye intensely studies this nearly ten-foot-wide painting during a scene set at the Art Institute. Featuring people of every age and social class on the banks of the River Seine, A Sunday on La Grande Jatte—1884 has captivated visitors ever since its arrival at the museum in 1924.

If we, like Cameron, come closer to the painting, figures and forms dissolve into dots and dashes of complementary colors laid side by side, characteristic of Seurat’s pointillist technique. Many smaller painted and drawn sketches and several larger canvases, in which Seurat laid out the parameters for the landscape and figures, led up to this majestically composed scene. Seurat returned to the work two years after its start date, amplifying the silhouettes of some figures and adding others. Some of these, like the monkey on the leash, seem so integral to the final composition that it is hard to imagine them as add-ons, but others, like the man carrying a rolled newspaper in the furthest distance, are barely noticeable. To the artist, however, every decision was essential to his aim of making a painting of modern life equivalent to a classical Greek frieze.

16410.alt: A work made of oil on panel.
16410.short:
A woman in a white cap and apron leans over a wooden barrel in a dim, barn-like room with heavy wooden beams. Around her the floor is crowded with household things: wooden tubs, earthenware jugs and pots, a large wicker basket, a metal plate and a blue-and-white china plate. Bones and an animal skull lie on the floor, and a cat sleeps in the lower right corner. A rooster stands on the left, and a hen perches on top of the basket on the right.

Hendrik Martensz. Sorgh painted this oil on panel in 1657.

561.title: The Family Concert
561.caption: Jan Steen. The Family Concert, 1666. The Art Institute of Chicago.
561.alt: Painting of several light-skinned people gathered around a table in front of a gilded mirror, playing instruments. At left, seated next to a woman in an off-the-shoulder gown, a man in a plumed hat plays a lute. At center right, another man plays a cello, while a dog and cat eat from a dish underfoot.
561.short: This well-appointed interior sets the scene for the courtship ritual of music-making, through which men and women became acquainted by singing and playing instruments together. Jan Steen, one of the Dutch Republic’s most prolific comic painters, crafted his scenes upon the contemporary notion that comedy mirrors everyday life.

117476.title: Merrymakers in an Inn
117476.caption: Adriaen van Ostade. Merrymakers in an Inn, 1674. The Art Institute of Chicago.
117476.alt: A work made of oil on panel.
117476.short: Over the course of a long and successful career in Haarlem, Adriaen van Ostade specialized in scenes of peasant life, including tavern scenes and village fairs. This late painting combines elements from both types, like smoking and drinking figures and musicians serenading a dancing couple. The artist used clear, relatively bright colors and fine brushwork, in keeping with the market demand of the later 1600s. Collectors also appreciated the range of emotions and gestures exhibited by Van Ostade’s jolly figures.

512.title: The Music Lesson

512.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
512.short: In this small-scale scene of everyday life, a woman plays the double-headed lute as her companion marks the tempo. Gerard ter Borch the Younger painted many images like this one, featuring military officers and elegant young women in shimmering satin conversing, making music, or exchanging letters.

Warm, cloudy light fills the sky.

Richard Parkes Bonington painted this view in oil on millboard in 1826.

16417.caption: David Teniers the Younger. The Flageolet Player, 1635/40. The Art Institute of Chicago.

The room is dark, with light falling on the faces and the young man's sleeves.

81568.title: Notre Dame de Paris
81568.caption: Jean-François Rafaëlli. Notre Dame de Paris, c. 1890. The Art Institute of Chicago.
81568.alt: A work made of oil on composition board.
81568.short:
The towers and spire of Notre-Dame cathedral rise across the river in Paris. On the riverside walk in the foreground, two nuns in black habits and white headdresses walk side by side. Nearby, a man sits beneath a tree with a small dog, and another pushes a handcart. Trees with brown autumn leaves line the embankment, a street lamp stands among them, and carriages cross the bridge in the distance. Fallen leaves cover the wet ground.

Jean François Raffaëlli painted this oil on composition board around 1890. It is signed in the lower left corner.

144969.title: The Interior of the Palm House on the Pfaueninsel Near Potsdam
144969.caption: Carl Blechen. The Interior of the Palm House on the Pfaueninsel Near Potsdam, 1834. The Art Institute of Chicago.
144969.alt: Four women with musical instruments lounge in a massive garden courtyard.
144969.short:
Lush palms and overgrown greenery dominate this view of the Palm House, designed by Karl Friedrich Schinkel to display the Prussian royals’ collection of tropical plants. This painting plays with the boundaries between architecture and nature, imagination and reality: vines curl around soaring columns and bowed fronds evoke archways. Carl Blechen populated his dazzling place-portrait with a leisure scene derived from colonialist fantasies of non-European women. The artist dressed the ﬁgures in rich textiles that echo the building’s colors and motifs, as if he considered them an extension of the decor.

The short career of Carl Blechen, a pivotal ﬁgure in nineteenth-century German painting, marked the transition from Romanticism to a more realistic view of nature. Inspired in part by his encounter with the Italian landscape and light during a trip he made around 1828 or 1829, Blechen developed a ﬂuid technique that enabled him to capture ﬂeeting atmospheric effects. He often used his landscapes as settings for mysterious ﬁgures, reﬂecting his early contact with Romantic painting and theater.

Behind them, a figure dressed in black walks past with a small dog, and a street of tall buildings and carriages stretches into the distance. The trees have only a few yellow leaves left, and the light is pale.

Jean François Raffaëlli painted this oil on panel around 1890. It is signed in the lower right corner.

Jean François Raffaëlli painted this oil on canvas around 1880. It is signed in the lower right corner.

111062.title: Te raau rahi (The Big Tree)
111062.caption: Paul Gauguin. Te raau rahi (The Big Tree), 1891. The Art Institute of Chicago.
111062.alt: A work made of oil on jute canvas.
111062.short: “Everything in the landscape blinded and dazzled me,” wrote Paul Gauguin of his first months in Tahiti. Here, he showcased the island’s variety of bountiful fruit trees, including a thick-trunked, violet hotu at left; spindly mango and coconut trees; and three short banana plants with lush, splayed leaves. In the foreground, a man uses a stick to crack a coconut and a family rests in the grass with a sleeping dog beside them. The painting’s coarsely woven canvas, made of a fibrous plant matter (jute), is visible through the paint layer. Cheaper and more readily available than traditional canvas, this support material lends the work a rugged, organic texture.

28560.title: The Bedroom
28560.caption: Vincent van Gogh. The Bedroom, 1889. The Art Institute of Chicago.
28560.alt: Painting of bedroom, blue walls, green window, tan bed, red bedding.
28560.short:
Perhaps the most famous depiction of a bedroom in Western art history, this vibrant painting documents Vincent van Gogh’s sleeping quarters in his beloved “Yellow House” in Arles, France. The composition exists in three versions, the first of which Van Gogh conceived in October 1888, a month after he moved into the home. In a letter to his brother Theo, he described having painted “the walls pale lilac, the floor in a broken and faded red, the chairs and the bed chrome yellow, the pillows and the sheet very pale lemon green, the bedspread blood-red, the dressing table orange, the washbasin blue, the window green.” With its bold colors, thick and broken brushwork, and sharply receding lines, the picture might suggest a nervous energy. But the artist understood it as a calming and restful image.

The painting in the Art Institute’s collection is Van Gogh’s second version of the scene, made nearly a year after the first, in September 1889. He produced a third, smaller version at the same time as a gift for his mother and sister.

Shadows of leaves fall across the pillars.

Thomas Fearnley painted this oil on paper, later mounted on canvas, around 1834. It is signed in the lower right corner.

44742.title: Are They Thinking about the Grape? (Pensent-ils au raisin?)
44742.caption: François Boucher. Are They Thinking about the Grape? (Pensent-ils au raisin?), 1747. The Art Institute of Chicago.
44742.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
44742.short: This painting is based on a 1745 pantomime about a young shepherd’s awakening love for a shepherdess. The couple feed each other grapes—a fruit associated with Bacchus, god of pleasure—suggesting that their encounter is not entirely chaste. François Boucher’s compositions on pastoral themes comprise his most influential contribution to 18th-century French art. These lush and playful fantasies of rustic life, designed primarily for the private enjoyment of wealthy financiers and aristocrats, had little to do with the social realities of rural labor during the period.

16496.title: No te aha oe riri (Why Are You Angry?)
16496.caption: Paul Gauguin. No te aha oe riri (Why Are You Angry?), 1896. The Art Institute of Chicago.
16496.alt: A work made of oil on jute canvas.
16496.short: In this large-scale canvas, one of several Paul Gauguin sent back to France in 1897, women of varying ages appear to go about daily life within a colorful, stylized outdoor environment. Like much of the artist’s work, this painting combines observed detail with artistic fantasy to create a dreamlike scene whose narrative resists simple interpretation. The work’s deliberately provocative title enhances this effect, leaving us to wonder if the “you” refers to someone in the painting or to the viewer.

16398.caption: Jacob Ochtervelt. The Music Lesson, 1671. The Art Institute of Chicago.
16398.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.

The artist positioned the figures in angled poses suggesting a playful interaction. The girl holds a violin, an instrument then more often played by men, and points authoritatively to the music score, another reversal of typical gender roles for the period. By upending these conventions, Ochtervelt quietly commented on the rituals of romance in the 17th century.

20684.title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
20684.caption: Gustave Caillebotte. Paris Street; Rainy Day, 1877. The Art Institute of Chicago.
20684.alt: Life-size painting of an urban scene in Paris. A man in a top hat holding an umbrella and a woman in a long fashionable dark dress walk arm in arm toward the viewer as other city dwellers with umbrellas walk in various directions across cobblestone roads and sidewalks.
20684.short:
This monumental painting is Gustave Caillebotte’s largest, most ambitious work and has been a visitor favorite since the Art Institute acquired it in 1964, well before the artist’s contributions to the Impressionist movement were widely recognized. Caillebotte captured a busy intersection of Paris that was only a short walk from his home. In fact, his paintings of Paris rarely depict areas beyond his familiar neighborhoods.

Caillebotte demonstrated his affinity with the Impressionists through his subject of modern urban life but approached these settings with a more Realist technique. The dramatic cropping of the scene may have been inspired by the newly popularized medium of photography; the two central figures seem to be walking straight into the viewer as something captures their attention outside of the frame. 160032.title: The Festival
160032.caption: Sir John Edward Poynter. The Festival, 1875. The Art Institute of Chicago.
160032.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
160032.short:
Two women decorate a room with roses in this tall, narrow painting. One stands on a ladder against a white column, wearing a pale robe, an olive-green drape and a gold band in her hair, and she reaches down for a garland of roses and leaves. Below her, a second woman in white kneels and lifts the garland up to her, holding a long yellow ribbon. Behind them are red walls and carved columns. A basket full of roses sits at the lower left, more roses lie scattered across the mosaic floor, and a dark glass vase stands on the right.

Edward John Poynter painted this oil on canvas in 1875. It carries his monogram and the date in the lower left corner.

117477.caption: François Bonvin. The Maid, c. 1875. The Art Institute of Chicago.
117477.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
117477.short: This maid pours blood from a flayed ox’s head as she prepares to make a delicacy known as headcheese. Such paintings of everyday life were popular in late 19th-century France; as the nation experienced rapid industrialization and urbanization, audiences appreciated imagery that romanticized traditional rural life, with its perceived simplicity and virtuousness. François Bonvin regularly executed genre scenes reminiscent of works by 18th-century French artist Jean Siméon Chardin, who also celebrated the quiet dignity of domestic labor.

16347.title: An Elegant Company
16347.caption: Pieter Codde. An Elegant Company, 1632. The Art Institute of Chicago.
16347.alt: A work made of oil on panel.
16347.short: A master of scenes of finely dressed revelers known as “merry companies,” Amsterdam painter Pieter Codde here demonstrated his sharp sense of composition. He animated a gathering of 18 guests and attendants through a complex network of gestures, glances, and poses, with a young woman dressed in luxurious silver satin at center. Such images of joyful gatherings, with participants acting in accordance with their privileged social station, would have functioned as models of polite behavior to cosmopolitan art collectors.

81555.title: Lunch at the Restaurant Fournaise (The Rowers' Lunch)
81555.caption: Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Lunch at the Restaurant Fournaise (The Rowers' Lunch), 1875. The Art Institute of Chicago.
81555.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
81555.short:
Three people sit over the remains of lunch under a green trellis arbour beside a river. On the left, a bearded man in a light jacket faces a woman in a dark dress, who sits with her back to us. On the right, a man in a white shirt leans back in his chair with one hand raised. The tablecloth holds bottles, wine glasses and a plate with a bunch of grapes. Beyond the trellis, red flowers bloom and rowing boats glide across the bright, shimmering water.

Pierre-Auguste Renoir painted this oil on canvas in 1875. It is inscribed "Renoir" in the lower left corner.

16571.title: Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare
16571.caption: Claude Monet. Arrival of the Normandy Train, Gare Saint-Lazare, 1877. The Art Institute of Chicago.
16571.alt: Loosely painted image of an open-air train station. On the right, a parked train gives off an enormous plumb of white smoke, making the scene look as though it were full of clouds. A huddled mass of barely discernible people crowd around the train on both sides of the tracks. Blue, green, and gray tones dominate.
16571.short:
One of the most avant-garde aspects of the Impressionists was their choice of subject matter, which frequently included scenes derived from modern, industrial Paris, from iron bridges to exhibition halls to train sheds. The train station at Saint-Lazare would have been a familiar, meaningful sight to Claude Monet in the 1870s. The terminal linked Paris to Normandy, where the artist developed his technique of painting outdoors in the 1860s. It was also the point of departure for the towns and villages west and north of Paris that the Impressionists frequently visited. Monet completed eight of his twelve known paintings of the Gare Saint-Lazare in time for the third Impressionist exhibition, in 1877, probably displaying them in the same gallery.

Monet chose to focus his attention here on the glass-and-iron train shed, where he found an appealing combination of artiﬁ cial and natural effects—the rising steam of locomotives trapped within the structure and the daylight penetrating large, glazed sections of the roof, for instance. Monet’s depictions of the station inaugurated what was to become for him an established pattern of painting a speciﬁc motif repeatedly in order to capture subtle and temporal atmospheric changes, as in his famous series of stacks of wheat. But the Saint-Lazare paintings also represented his last attempt to capture urban life: from this point on in his career, Monet largely devoted himself to landscapes.

27984.title: Woman before an Aquarium
27984.caption: Henri Matisse. Woman before an Aquarium, 1921–23. The Art Institute of Chicago.
27984.alt: Painting of woman, arms crossed on brown desk, staring at goldfish.
27984.short: In the first two decades of the 20th century, Henri Matisse visited exhibitions of Islamic art and traveled to Algeria and Morocco, where he collected pottery, textiles, and tiles. Years later while living in Nice, France, Matisse reflected on these experiences, integrating visual elements he encountered, such as the patterned textile screen, into his paintings. In Woman before an Aquarium, the carefully subdued decorative pattern of the screen contributes to the psychologically rich, contemplative mood of this interior scene.

80475.title: Ice-Bound Falls
80475.caption: Ernest Lawson. Ice-Bound Falls, 1919. The Art Institute of Chicago.
80475.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
80475.short:
A waterfall tumbles over dark rocks, half buried in snow and ice, into a swirling green pool. Snow covers the banks on both sides. Above the falls stand a long pink building and a smaller house, and another small pink building sits on the rocks at the lower left. Behind them, dark conifers climb the slopes of a snowy mountain under a pale sky. The paint is laid on in thick, broken strokes of white, blue and violet.

Ernest Lawson painted this oil on canvas in 1919. It is signed and dated in the lower right corner.

111617.title: Cabin in the Cotton
111617.caption: Horace Pippin. Cabin in the Cotton, c. 1931–37. The Art Institute of Chicago.
111617.alt: Painting of a cabin set below a dark blue sky and fluffy white clouds. Behind it is a field of many small white dots. In front, a dark-skinned woman sits and a dark-skinned child plays among roaming chickens and dogs in a fenced-in yard.
111617.short: Constructed of dense, thick layers of paint, Cabin in the Cotton exemplifies the tactile and vivid style of selftaught artist Horace Pippin. At a southern homestead, an older woman cares for a young child. Beyond, an expansive field of cotton evokes the hard labor, likely that of family members, required to harvest the crop. Pippin turned to painting as a mode of rehabilitation after injuring his arm while serving in World War I. Born in Pennsylvania, the artist’s interpretation of cotton fields drew upon a visit to South Carolina with his regiment in 1917. Popular culture also may have informed his work: “Cabin in the Cotton” was the title of both a song and a film in the 1930s. On view in a shoe repair shop outside Philadelphia in 1937, the composition caught the attention of artists, critics, and gallerists, winning Pippin wide acclaim and furthering his career.

81539.title: On the Bank of the Seine, Bennecourt
81539.caption: Claude Monet. On the Bank of the Seine, Bennecourt, 1868. The Art Institute of Chicago.
81539.alt: Painting of woman in a striped dress seated on the bank of a river, beneath a full, leafy tree, a boat at the shore and a village visible across the river.
81539.short: Here Claude Monet’s future wife, Camille Doncieux, sits on an island in the Seine River, looking toward the hamlet of Gloton, next to the town of Bennecourt, from which she and Monet have presumably rowed. This is the only painting to survive from the brief period that the couple spent in Gloton, which the novelist Émile Zola recommended to Monet as a cheap rural retreat that was easily accessible from Paris. Pentimenti (visible traces of earlier painting beneath a layer or layers of paint) suggest that in an early stage of the painting, Camille held a bonneted child, presumably the couple’s baby, Jean.

133859.title: Lady Reading the Letters of Heloise and Abelard
133859.caption: Bernard d'Agescy. Lady Reading the Letters of Heloise and Abelard, c. 1780. The Art Institute of Chicago.
133859.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
133859.short: This painting depicts a young woman lost in reverie after reading the letters of the ill-fated medieval lovers Heloise and Abelard. The objects on the table beside her—a letter, a sheet of music, and a book of erotic poetry—hint at a life of leisure and a susceptibility to love. In this early picture, Auguste Bernard drew upon history paintings by Peter Paul Rubens and Charles Le Brun, as well as Parisian traditions of genre painting and portraiture pioneered by Jean-Baptiste Greuze. Bernard worked in Paris in the early 1780s and studied in Italy for several years. Upon his return to Paris, he found his career frustrated by the French Revolution and the emergent fashion for the more austere Neoclassical style.

81521.title: The Woodchopper
81521.caption: Jean François Millet. The Woodchopper, c. 1858–66. The Art Institute of Chicago.
81521.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
81521.short:
A young man in a pale shirt raises a heavy axe high above his head, about to bring it down. Beside him is a large pile of split wood, with a hat and a blue cloth lying on top and another axe leaning against it. On the right, a saw rests on a wooden sawhorse, and thick logs lie on the ground. Behind him, a dark wall of forest fills most of the picture, with a strip of grey sky at the top.

Jean-François Millet painted this oil on canvas around 1858 to 1866. It is stamped "J.F. Millet" in the lower right corner.

70118.title: Old Man Lighting a Pipe
70118.caption: Johann Carl Loth. Old Man Lighting a Pipe, c. 1660. The Art Institute of Chicago.
70118.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
70118.short: This man’s suntanned skin, worn clothing, and rustic surroundings are rendered in shades of brown that mirror the contents of his pipe. The Spanish introduced tobacco into Northern Europe in the 16th century, and smoking quickly became a beloved pastime that was widely considered healthful and nourishing. By the early 17th century, single-figure images of smokers emerged as a subgenre of Dutch and Flemish painting. The theme posed an enticing challenge for artists, with its burning leaves, billowing plumes of smoke, and active facial expressions—here, the figure purses his lips and wrinkles his brow as he concentrates on lighting the pipe. German painter Johann Carl Loth blended the Northern emphasis on capturing textures with the dramatic illumination reminiscent of so-called Caravaggesque painters like Hendrick Terbrugghen.

117700.title: On the Bank
117700.caption: Frederick Carl Frieseke. On the Bank, c. 1915. The Art Institute of Chicago.
117700.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.
117700.short:
A nude woman in a cap sits on a patterned cloth on a riverbank, seen from behind, with her knees drawn up and her hands raised to her head. Beside her, an open parasol with a striped border lies on the ground, and a straw hat trimmed with flowers rests on the cloth. Sunlight flickers through the leaves onto her back and sparkles on the water beyond. The whole picture is built up from small dabs of pale blue, green and yellow.

Frederick Carl Frieseke painted this oil on canvas around 1915. It is signed in blue paint on the grass in the lower right corner.

21165.alt: A work made of oil on canvas.

Trees and a cloudy sky fill the background, and the paint is applied in quick, loose strokes.

Marcellin Gilbert Desboutin painted this oil on canvas between 1875 and 1879. It is signed in the lower right corner.

11723.title: Woman at Her Toilette
11723.caption: Berthe Morisot. Woman at Her Toilette, 1875–80. The Art Institute of Chicago.
11723.alt: Painted portrait dominated by loose, large brushstrokes of a woman, seen from the back, wearing a gauzy white off-the-shoulder dress and black choker, blond hair swept up, examining herself in a mirror at left. The background is a feathered swirl suggesting floral pattern in cool pale tones of gray, purple, pink, and blue.
11723.short:
In Woman at Her Toilette, Berthe Morisot provided a glimpse into the private life of a Parisienne—one of the fashionable, urban women who epitomized modernity in late nineteenth-century France. The ﬁgure is shown at her vanity table after a ball, still wearing her earrings and a velvet ribbon around her neck as she reaches up to take down her chignon hairstyle. In the background, Morisot’s soft, feathery brushstrokes suggest a ﬂ oral-patterned bedspread and wallpaper. The artist applied the same gauzy technique to the mirror, obscuring the ﬁ gure’s reﬂection and thus disrupting the trope of women gazing into mirrors as a symbol of vanity. Morisot signed her name along the bottom of the mirror, an enigmatic detail that may suggest that the ﬁgure is a stand-in for the artist herself.

Consistent with the Impressionist aesthetic that Morisot fervently espoused, In Woman at Her Toilette attempts to capture the essence of modern life in summary, understated terms. Morisot exhibited in seven of the eight Impressionist group shows; in 1880 this painting was included in the ﬁfth exhibition, where her work received high acclaim. In addition to domestic interiors such as this one, Morisot’s pictorial realm included studies of women and children, gardens, ﬁelds, and vacation homes by the sea.
